items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: stories of Lester Young and Don Byas or Buddy Tate not liking one another

ctx.x: In the old days, Basie liked to keep something going like stories of Lester Young and Don Byas or Buddy Tate not liking one another, but they were all, they really loved each other. But the stories were about the rivalry going on.

Well that was the thing from those days, you know, guys would purposely, you know, go out looking for a session, for one particular guy, for the cutting contests. That doesn’t happen much anymore, but I mean they would take it through all sorts of things I suppose, you know, changing keys, and tunes and if you couldn’t hang, you were dead. But I remember this one particular instance, we were doing a Birdland show. And I don’t remember, I remember we flew up to Boston and we did the show, and then we flew right…

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: I liked Buddy Tate more at the time... I think he got a kick out of that, between Lester Young and Buddy Tate.

ctx.x: So you saw some of the great saxophone sections coming through there.

Yes, yes. Benny Carter had a — oh my goodness, he had a lead alto player named Porter Kilbourn who was almost as ferocious as he himself was. And of course the great Duke Ellington had Johnny Hodges and Otto Hardwick and Harry Carney. And of course the Basie saxophone section with Earle Warren, Tab Smith, Don Byas, or Buddy Tate and Lester Young.
So you got to hear Lester in the Basie band?

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: veering back and forth between Prez and Don Byas and Buddy Tate

ctx.x: I think it was Miles first. I think it was Miles, Monk, Miles.

Miles, Monk, Miles, yeah. Before his first tour of duty with Miles, his style and my style were very similar. This is around 1954, I think, ’55. I remember hearing a recording of his and I remember remarking to myself, wow, he sounds a lot like me. Then he got with Miles and I with Basie, and our paths went in vastly different directions. Trying to fit with the Basie orchestra and being torn between the Lester Young approach, and the Buddy Tate, Don Byas approach, and really being in love with Sonny Stitt, I was…
I don’t know about that, but that’s -­

items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: And Frank Foster. He was just there and I called him up and Arnett and it was on the last set and we got into a thing... we just felt a groove and we just really swung

ctx.x: Joe Farrell, yeah, Joe Farrell. And Frank Foster. He was just there and I called him up and Arnett and it was on the last set and we got into a thing, man, that may never happen again in life. We had everybody screaming, man, in that place and nobody was really trying to out -- really trying -- we just felt a groove and we just really swung and man, we had a standing ovation. That was the last tune that we all -- you know, like I called everybody out and I was sort of like the emcee and of course, Richie had just…
Do you listen to your own records much?
